Quantum Interfaces: transferring quantum information between light and matter

Lecture 2: The platforms, the links and what limits them

Shayne Bennetts

IAMS Yb Lab, Institute of Atomic and Molecular Sciences, Academia Sinica

TIGP, Tuesday 24 November 2026

2.5-2
2.5

Linking nodes: repeaters and heralded entanglement

Fibre loss · atom-photon entanglement · Hong-Ou-Mandel · one click or two · linked atomic clouds · teleportation · the repeater · distillation · memories · link rate · frequency conversion

2.5

Entangling two nodes by photons at a beam splitter

  • Nodes A and B, L apart, send photons to a beam splitter with two detectors
  • C1 or β says how well each node couples to its mode
  • η is the fraction of photons collected, transmitted and detected
  • The rate of pairs is the probability per attempt times the attempt rate
  • ηlink=γent/γdec is the rate of pairs over the rate at which the memories lose them
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.5-1

A photon's survival in fibre falls exponentially with length

T=e−L/Latt=10−αL/10
  • Latt is the attenuation length; α is the loss in dB/km
  • At 854 nm, about 3 dB/km, a photon survives 50 km with probability 10−15
  • At 1550 nm the loss is 0.181 dB/km, but the fall is still exponential
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317; Duan et al., Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105, p. 5
2.5-3

The solution is repeaters

T=e−L/Latt=10−αL/10
  • Latt is the attenuation length; α is the loss in dB/km
  • At 854 nm, about 3 dB/km, a photon survives 50 km with probability 10−15
  • At 1550 nm the loss is 0.181 dB/km, but the fall is still exponential
  • In segments L0 and then joined (dashed), it falls only as a power: (L0/L)2
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317; Duan et al., Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105, p. 5
2.5-25

A decaying atom leaves its qubit entangled with its photon

|Ψ⟩AP=(|↓⟩|L⟩+|↑⟩|R⟩)/2
  • A 87Rb atom in mF=0 is excited to |e⟩, which has F′=0
  • A decay to mF=−1, called |↓⟩, emits a left-circular photon |L⟩
  • A decay to mF=+1, called |↑⟩, emits a right-circular photon |R⟩
  • Nothing records which decay happened, so atom A and photon P stay in superposition
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012), Fig. 1B; Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316
2.5-8

Two detected photons entangle the atoms that emitted them

  • Identical photons that arrive together leave the beam splitter by the same port
  • One photon in each output, H and V, leaves the atoms, which never met, in |Ψ−⟩
Hong, Ou and Mandel, Phys. Rev. Lett. 59, 2044 (1987), Fig. 2; Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012)
2.5-9

Fidelity: A pair is judged by its fidelity to a Bell state

  • The fidelity F is the overlap of the pair's measured state ρ with the target Bell state
  • F>0.5 proves two qubits are entangled
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012); Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 050803 (2023), arXiv:2208.14907; van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.5-10

Key terms:

  • Heralded means that a signal announces the pair, and the pair is kept for use
  • Post-selected means that only trials with both photons detected count, and no pair is left
  • Deterministic means that every trial delivers a pair
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012); Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 050803 (2023), arXiv:2208.14907; van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.5-26

One detected photon is enough to entangle two nodes

  • a, b: with a small probability p, a node's atom flips from ↓ to ↑ and emits a photon
  • c: one click cannot tell which node emitted, so a and b remain in superposition
  • The phase ϕ=ϕB−ϕA needs path lengths stable to a fraction of a wavelength
  • In a share p of the clicks both atoms flipped, giving a fidelity, F≈1−p
  • One photon must arrive: the rate goes as η, not as η2 as with two photons
Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373; Chen et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 022329 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0609151; Duan et al., Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105
2.5-12

Single photon wins at low efficiency, two photons at high

Single Photon: H1=2P×0.1
Two Photon: H2=P2/2
  • H1 and H2 are the chances per attempt of a herald by one click and by two photons
  • P is the probability that one node's photon is generated, transmitted and detected
  • Example: For single photon, each node emits with p=0.1, so that F≈1−p=0.9
  • At P=0.01 and 2 kHz, single photon gives 4 heralds a second, two photons 0.1
  • Above P=0.4 (calculated) the two-photon herald wins!
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317
2.5-13

Recall: A cavity reflects only if an atom inside couples

  • The cavity is built so that a photon on resonance enters and is lost: no click (a)
  • An atom in |1⟩ splits the resonance by 2g: the photon is reflected, a click (b)
  • A click says that at least one atom is in |1⟩. It does not say which
Sørensen and Mølmer, Phys. Rev. Lett. 90, 127903 (2003), arXiv:quant-ph/0206142; Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702; the reflection of lecture 1
2.5-27

State carving: Two clicks carve an entangled pair out of four possibilities

Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702, Eq. 1; Sørensen and Mølmer, Phys. Rev. Lett. 90, 127903 (2003), arXiv:quant-ph/0206142; panel f: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316
2.7-18

One photon passing twice leaves a Bell state at every click

Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702, Eq. 2
2.7-19

A modest cavity is enough: C₁ ≈ 17 for 0.999, calculated

  • The error of the heralded pair falls as 1/C12 (a): 0.999 at C1≈17 [the paper's 4g2/(κγ)≈34]
  • An error falling as 1/C1 would need C1≈500 for 0.999 (dashed)
  • A lost photon gives no click, so loss lowers the success (b), not the fidelity
  • With 2 % of the light lost in the cavity the success stays above 0.9
Goswami et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 050802 (2026), arXiv:2505.02702, Eq. 3, a proposal
2.7-20

Measuring the inner atoms joins two short links into one

  • Each short link is tried on its own, so no photon travels further than L0
  • Repeated, the step doubles the distance each time
  • Loss lengthens the wait T0~tΔ/(ηppc), for attempts of length tΔ and efficiency ηp
  • Joined efficiently, the time grows as (L/L0)2
Briegel et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 5932 (1998), arXiv:quant-ph/9803056; Duan et al., Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105
2.5-20

How it works: we teleport qubit 1 to qubit 3

Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 70, 1895 (1993); Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012)
2.5-11

Which detectors click decides what the receiver does

What clicksWhat it meansThe receiver applies
H and V in different outputssuccessa flip and a sign change
H and V in the same outputsuccessa flip
two photons in one detector, or a photon lostno resultnothing: the state is lost
  • A beam splitter tells apart two of the four possible results, so this works at most half of the time
  • Each success comes one time in four, whatever the state was: the clicks reveal nothing about it
  • Three ions in one trap, each read directly (2004): all four results, fidelity 75 %; without the pair, 2/3 at best
Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 70, 1895 (1993); Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012); Riebe et al., Nature 429, 734 (2004); Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373; Main et al., Nature 638, 383 (2025), arXiv:2407.00835
2.5-21

A memory turns a chance of p² per attempt into about p

⟨N⟩a=1p2,⟨N⟩b=3−2pp(2−p)≈32p
  • Each of two segments heralds a pair (orange dot) with probability p per attempt
  • ⟨N⟩ is the mean number of attempts until both hold a pair
  • a: without memories, both must succeed in the same attempt
  • b: a memory keeps the first pair (blue bar) until the second arrives
  • Two ions, 25 km to each side: 7.2×10−6 per attempt without memory, 9.2×10−4 with it
Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 213601 (2023), arXiv:2210.05418, p. 3 and Supplemental Material, Eq. S4
2.5-6

A repeater joins short entangled links into one long one

  • Each segment of length L0, about one Latt, is entangled on its own and kept until needed
  • A Bell measurement at an orange node swaps two pairs into one twice as long
  • Purification makes one better pair from two noisy ones, as distillation shows later
  • Purifying and swapping in turn, the cost grows only as a power of distance
  • Errors of a percent in each node's operations are tolerated
Briegel, Dür, Cirac and Zoller, Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 5932 (1998), arXiv:quant-ph/9803056; Żukowski et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 71, 4287 (1993)
2.5-5

Distillation: two noisy pairs in, one better pair out

Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. A 54, 3824 (1996), arXiv:quant-ph/9604024; Dür et al., Phys. Rev. A 59, 169 (1999), arXiv:quant-ph/9808065
2.5-23

One case worked through: an error of 10 % falls to about 1 %

The two pairsHow oftenThe two detectorsWhat happens
both right81 %both click, or neitherpair 1 is kept, and it is right
one of them wrong18 %only one clicksboth are thrown away
both wrong1 %both click, or neitherpair 1 is kept, but it is wrong
  • 82 % of attempts are kept, and 81 in 82 of those are right: the error falls from 10 % to 1.2 %
  • With every kind of error present, one round takes F from 0.90 to 0.93, so the step is repeated
  • The gates add errors of their own: simple schemes stop at about ten times the gate error
Calculated here for the step of Dür et al., Phys. Rev. A 59, 169 (1999), arXiv:quant-ph/9808065; Ramette et al., npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296
2.5-24

Larger schemes are calculated to reach errors of 2 × 10⁻⁴

  • Both nodes make the same checks on n pairs; the box is the two-pair step
  • With perfect gates, the two-pair step purifies errors below 50 %
  • On a mismatch the nodes discard (heralded) or correct (deterministic)
  • A large code: each pair of error 2×10−4 from 3.6 pairs of 5 % error (calculated)
Bonilla Ataides et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 130804 (2025), arXiv:2502.09542, Table II; Ramette et al., npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296; Dür et al., Phys. Rev. A 59, 169 (1999), arXiv:quant-ph/9808065; Bennett et al., Phys. Rev. A 54, 3824 (1996), arXiv:quant-ph/9604024
2.5-17

A link is useful when it makes pairs faster than its memories lose them

  • Attempts at rate f for a fraction d of the time, each heralding with P=η2/2, give R=fPd
  • ηlink=γent/γdec=RT2; above one, pairs come faster than they decay
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088; Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Hucul et al., Nat. Phys. 11, 37 (2015), arXiv:1403.3696; van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526
2.5-16

Converted to 1550 nm, an 854 nm photon survives better beyond about 2 km

  • a: in a χ(2) crystal a strong 1902 nm pump turns an 854 nm photon into 1550 nm
  • The pump's Raman scattering adds noise photons
  • The fibre loses about 0.1 dB/m at 369.5 nm and 3 dB/km at 854 nm
  • b: the dashed curve is 854 nm light converted with 25 % efficiency
  • For 854 nm, conversion pays beyond the dot, near 2 km (calculated)
Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), for 369.5 nm; Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317, for 854 nm, 1550 nm and the conversion
2.5-18

A satellite avoids the exponential loss of fibre

  • One photon of each pair goes down to each of two stations 1203 km apart
  • The two downlinks, 1600 to 2400 km together, lose 64 to 82 dB (orange box)
  • Against 1200 km of fibre (blue line), the link gains 12 to 17 orders of magnitude
  • 5.9×106 pairs per second at the source, about 1.1 per second reach both stations
  • Post-selected fidelity F≥0.87±0.09; CHSH S=2.37±0.09, above the classical bound 2
Yin et al., Science 356, 1140 (2017), arXiv:1707.01339, Fig. 4

2.6-19

The mirror losses, not the coupling, cost the photons

κoutκ=T1T1+T2+ℓ≈0.16
  • The output mirror transmits T1 = 13 ppm, the other T2 = 1.3 ppm
  • The two mirrors lose ℓ = 68 ppm between them
  • So a photon leaves through the output mirror with probability κout/κ, only 16 % (a)
  • The detectors register 40 % of those: 6.4 % expected, 5.7 % measured (b)
  • Fixed in 2019 with a more transmitting output mirror: about 80 % leave
Stute et al., Nature 485, 482 (2012), arXiv:1301.0275; κout/κ as in Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 13; Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317
2.6-5
2.6-20
2.6-21

Frequency conversion to carry the photon 50 km

  • Transmission ≫ 100 m in fibre requires conversion to telecom wavelengths (1.3/1.55 µm), otherwise losses are too high
  • The output mirror transmits 97 ppm, the losses 17 ppm: up to 83 % of photons leave
  • C1=1.47±0.03; the 854 nm photon is converted to 1550 nm, 25 % efficiently
  • After 50.47 km of fibre at 0.181 dB/km, ion-photon F=0.86±0.03, post-selected
  • 5.3×10−4 per attempt at 2.2 kHz: about one detected photon a second
  • Problem left: the converter passes 25 %, the detector counts 10 %
Figure: Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317, Fig. 1 (CC BY 4.0); fibre losses as in section 2.5
2.6-7

Two cavity nodes in buildings 230 m apart are entangled

WindowHeralded F (%)Rate
1 µs88.0−4.7+2.23.5 min−1
Full58.7−2.1+1.70.49 s−1
  • Two such nodes 230 m apart send their photons through 520 m of fibre (a, b)
  • Two clicks came in 0.033 % of the attempts, as often as through the best lenses
  • A narrow window keeps the photons that interfere best: higher F, lower rate
  • Problem left: weak coupling makes slow, unequal photons; an attempt takes 420 µs
Figure: Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 050803 (2023), arXiv:2208.14907, Fig. 1, satellite image Google Earth, Landsat / Copernicus
2.6-8

A lens straight into fibre gives 182 pairs a second at 94 %

  • 88Sr+ ions 2 m apart; an NA 0.6 lens couples about 4 % of the light into fibre
  • With 65 % detectors a photon is counted with 2.1 to 2.4 %, five times 2015
  • 2.18×10−4 per attempt, 833 000 attempts a second: 182 pairs a second
  • Heralded F = 94.0(5) %; each ion and its photon, 97.7 to 97.9 %
  • Problem left: the attempts pause to recool; blue light loses 30 dB/km in fibre
Figure: Stephenson et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 110501 (2020), arXiv:1911.10841, Fig. 3
2.6-14

Lens links gained five orders of magnitude in eighteen years

  • Each point is a heralded link between two ions, with its fidelity and what was changed
  • A coolant ion lets the attempts run without pauses: 250 s−1 (2024, one trap)
  • A second species holds the memory: 96.89(8) % at 9.7 s−1, and a gate was teleported (2025)
  • Photons that carry the qubit in their arrival time: 97.0(4) % at 0.35 s−1 (2025)
  • Problem left: a lens collects 10 to 20 % of the light at best; a photon is counted with about 2 %
Stephenson et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 110501 (2020), arXiv:1911.10841; O'Reilly et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 090802 (2024), arXiv:2404.16167; Main et al., Nature 638, 383 (2025), arXiv:2407.00835; Saha et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2533 (2025), arXiv:2406.01761; the other points as on their own slides

Conversion to a telecom wavelength reaches 33 km

  • Now each 780 nm photon is converted to 1517 nm, a telecom wavelength, at 57 %
  • Nodes 400 m apart; heralded fidelity ≥ 0.830(10) at 6 km, one pair per 19 s
  • At 33 km: ≥ 0.622(15), above one half, one pair per 208 s
  • Problem left: the lens collects few photons; the memory lasts T2≈330 µs
Figure: van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526, Fig. 1, CC BY 4.0
2.7-6

Ytterbium emits at 1389 nm, and five atoms run in parallel

  • Now ¹⁷¹Yb: ³D₁ decays to ³P₀ at 1389 nm, a telecom wavelength, so no converter is needed
  • And one objective images five atoms in tweezers onto five fibres: five attempts at once
  • Atom-photon fidelity 0.90(1), on the photons detected; the rate stays below 1 Hz
  • Problem left: only 0.5 % of the light reaches a fibre; a cavity could raise this to about 50 %
Figure: Li et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025), arXiv:2502.17406, Fig. 1a

Six atoms in one cavity yield a photon in 88.6 % of attempts

  • Now tweezers set up to six ⁸⁷Rb atoms 5.5 µm apart across one cavity's mode
  • One atom gives a detected photon in 33.2(2) % of attempts
  • Its atom-photon fidelity is 86.6(5) %, on the photons detected
  • The atoms emit in turn; with six, 88.6(1) % of attempts give a photon
  • Problem left: a mode waist of 30 µm gives C1≈1.7; off-centre atoms couple less
Figure: Hartung et al., Science 385, 179 (2024), arXiv:2407.09109, Fig. 1A

2.7-39

A 9.5 µm waist gives sixteen atoms C₁ near 50 (preprint)

  • Now mirrors of 1 mm radius, 1.67 mm apart: a waist of 9.5 µm, not 30 µm
  • Tweezers from above place a chain of ⁸⁷Rb atoms along the cavity axis (b), imaged in (c)
  • One atom has C1 = 56.2(1.7) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ) = 112.3 ± 3.3]
  • Sixteen atoms at the antinodes keep a mean C1 of 47.9(5) [95.7 ± 0.9]
  • Problem left: only transmission spectra so far; nothing entangled yet
Figure: Ye et al., arXiv:2607.04090 (2026), preprint, Fig. 1b and 1c
2.7-11

Lenses inside a cavity focus its mode far from every surface

  • Now a curved mirror and a lens, mm to cm away, focus the mode below a micron
  • The finesse is only 40, so the light passes the atom about ten times
  • From the vacuum Rabi splitting of one atom, C1 = 0.8(1) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ) = 1.6(2)]
  • Each atom gets its own mode (a); 21 are read at once (b), uncorrelated (c)
  • Problem left: C1 below 1; in an array the lenses cause most of the loss
Figure: Shaw et al., Nature 650, 320 (2026), arXiv:2506.10919, Fig. 1; Shadmany et al., Sci. Adv. 11, eads8171 (2025); Soper et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 041009 (2026), arXiv:2602.06587

A cavity inside the fibre puts the photon straight into it

  • Two fibre Bragg gratings 33 cm apart, round a 400 nm nanofibre, form the cavity
  • One trapped Cs atom couples strongly: (g0,κ,γ)/2π=(7.8,6.4,2.6) MHz, C1≈1.8
  • The authors estimate C1>150 with better tapers and gratings
  • Problem left: the tapers pass only 94 % of the light; an atom stays trapped 11 ms

A 1389 nm nanofibre cavity holds ytterbium for 6.8 s

Nanofibre cavities reach C₁ of 2 to 3; designs project far more

  • The chart: C1 on a log scale against the year; filled marks are measured
  • Two nanofibre cavities have measured C1≈1.8 (2015) and 2.7(3) (2019)
  • A preprint of 2026 has about 2.9, or 5.6(1.0) counting the internal loss alone
  • Designs project 90 and about 150 at 200 nm from the surface, 1050 at it
  • Chip cavities, the grey squares, have measured 13.5 and 36

2.8

Colour centres in diamond and quantum dots

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) links from one spin to two cities · silicon-vacancy (SiV) centres in nanocavities · quantum dots

2.8

The simplest node: one NV spin entangled with its photon

  • The simplest system: one NV in bulk diamond below 7 K, under an objective (b)
  • From A₂ it decays to |−1⟩ with σ+ light or to |+1⟩ with σ− light (a)
  • Spin-photon fidelity at least 0.69 ± 0.068
  • P≈10−6 per attempt at 100 kHz: one photon every few seconds
  • Problem left: only 4 % of the light is in the zero-phonon line (ZPL), and little of it is collected
Figure: Togan et al., Nature 466, 730 (2010), Fig. 1
2.8-2

Two NVs 1.3 km apart gave a loophole-free Bell test

  • The fix: a lens cut into the diamond over each NV, in labs 1280 m apart
  • Photons meet at C; an early and a late click herald Ψ−: fidelity 0.92 ± 0.03, estimated
  • The CHSH value S=2.42±0.20 beats 2, the bound of any local theory: 245 trials in 220 h
  • Problem left: both photons must arrive, so η enters squared: 6.4×10−9 per attempt
Figure: Hensen et al., Nature 526, 682 (2015), arXiv:1508.05949, Fig. 1c
2.8-3

A one-click herald entangles NVs faster than they decohere

  • The fix: one click heralds (section 2.5), so the rate goes as η, not η2
  • A photon is detected with P≈4×10−4, far below 0.4: one click is 1000 times faster
  • The price: a fibre stretcher holds the optical phase of the two paths (right)
  • Heralded: 0.81(2) at 6 Hz, 0.60(2) at 39 Hz, faster than a pair decoheres (5 Hz)
  • Problem left: the fidelity falls as the rate rises, and no second qubit stores a pair
Figure: Humphreys et al., Nature 558, 268 (2018), arXiv:1712.07567, Fig. 2b; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
2.8-4

A nuclear-spin memory joins three NV nodes

  • The fix: Bob stores one link in a 13C nuclear spin while he makes the next
  • Three NV nodes at 4 K in two labs, joined by 30 m and 2 m of fibre
  • Both links heralded: 0.820(5) at 9 Hz and 0.808(5) at 7 Hz
  • All three spins up plus all down, heralded: 0.538(18), once per 90 s
  • Problem left: the memory lasts about 1800 attempts, and all nodes are within 30 m
Figure: Pompili et al., Science 372, 259 (2021), arXiv:2102.04471, Fig. 1A; Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373
2.8-16

NV nodes in two cities 10 km apart are entangled

  • The fix of distance: each photon is converted from 637 nm to 1588 nm, where fibre loses little
  • Nodes 10 km apart, on 25 km of deployed fibre
  • Heralded Ψ−: fidelity 0.534(15) at 0.022 s−1
  • Noise counts cause about 30 % of the infidelity
  • Problem left: with no cavity, still only 4 % of the NV's light is in the ZPL
Figure: Stolk et al., Sci. Adv. 10, eadp6442 (2024), arXiv:2404.03723, Fig. 1; map tiles by CartoDB (CC BY 3.0), map data © OpenStreetMap contributors
2.8-17

A cavity needs a centre whose line stays put: the SiV

  • The fix, a nanocavity, puts the centre near surfaces with stray electric fields
  • Photons of two emitters interfere only if their lines stay matched (section 2.5)
  • The NV's permanent dipole makes its line follow stray fields (a, blue)
  • The symmetric silicon-vacancy centre, SiV, shifts only at second order (orange)
  • In b, a nucleus n stores the qubit, and each attempt by the electron e dephases it
Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), arXiv:1608.05147; Evans et al., Phys. Rev. Applied 5, 044010 (2016), arXiv:1512.03820; Pompili et al., Science 372, 259 (2021), arXiv:2102.04471
2.8-1

A nanocavity round an SiV reached C₁ ≈ 0.5 at 4 K

  • The fix: an SiV (orange) in a photonic-crystal cavity (A); C shows five such cavities
  • In F the line, of full width 2γ/2π = 298 MHz, broadens to 590 MHz on resonance
  • The line broadens by 1+2C1 (lecture 1), so C1≈0.5 [the paper's 4g2/(κγ)=1.0(1)]
  • Two SiVs in one waveguide reached F≥82(7) %, post-selected, at about 0.5 Hz
  • Problem left: at 4 K crystal vibrations disturb the SiV, and C₁ is below one
Figure: Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), arXiv:1608.05147, Fig. 1
2.8-6

Colder nodes and better cavities took C₁ from 0.5 to 52

r=2C1−12C1+1
  • The fix: nodes cooled below 0.3 K, and better cavities
  • r is the resonant reflection: −1 without the SiV, 0 at C1=1/2
  • C1 rose from about 0.5 in 2016 to 52±6 in 2020 [the paper's 105 ± 11]
  • Problem left: without a memory, two senders' photons must arrive in one attempt
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16; Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), arXiv:1608.05147; Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323; Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316
2.8-8

An SiV memory node beat direct transmission fourfold

  • The fix: the SiV spin holds one photon's state until the other arrives, in any later attempt
  • A and B send photons to an SiV in a cavity below 0.3 K, C1=52±6 [the paper's 105 ± 11]
  • The key rate was 4.1 ± 0.5 times p/2, the best without memory at transmission p
  • It beats 1.44p, the bound for any link without a repeater, with 99.2 % confidence
  • Problem left: one laboratory; the loss was emulated and one laser made both photons
Figure: Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323, Fig. 2a
2.8-10

A photon reflected off an SiV is entangled with its spin

  • At the probe frequency the cavity reflects only when the spin is up: 94 % against 4 %
  • Flipping the spin between a photon's early bin e and late bin l leaves (|e↓⟩+|l↑⟩)/2
  • Each box measures a photon in |±⟩=(|e⟩±|l⟩)/2, outcome ±1
  • In a, photons of A (1) and B (2) come at any times and leave their phases ϕ1, ϕ2 on the spin
  • The outcomes m1, m2 and, at (3), the spin's readout m3 give the photons' parity m1m2m3
  • In b, one photon reflected off A and B heralds Φ±
Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323; Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Eqs. 1 and 2
2.8-9

One reflected photon entangles two separate SiV nodes

  • The fix: two nodes in separate cryostats, linked by a pulse reflected off A, then B
  • At each node the electron spin meets the photon; a 29Si nucleus is the memory, T2=2.1 s
  • Heralded at mean photon number μ=0.017, about 16 mHz: Φ− 0.86(3), Φ+ 0.74(3)
  • For long fibre the photon is converted to 1350 nm and back; only 5.4 % passes
Figure: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Fig. 1, CC BY
2.8-11

Brighter pulses speed up the SiV link and lower its fidelity

  • Average fidelity against heralded rate; the inset shows Φ− and Φ+ at the lowest rate
  • Raising μ (top axis) lifts the rate from 16 mHz to 1.05 Hz, and the fidelity falls
  • The pair stays entangled, above 0.5 (dashed line), up to 1 Hz
  • Over a 35 km loop of deployed fibre: 0.69(7) at 0.23 mHz, heralded, with error detection
  • Problem left: conversion passes only 5.4 %, and the lines of the two SiVs differ by 13 GHz
Figure: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), arXiv:2310.01316, Fig. 2c, CC BY; Bersin et al., PRX Quantum 5, 010303 (2024), arXiv:2307.08619
2.8-12

In parallel, quantum dots entangle a spin with each photon

  • Left: a dot in a micropillar cavity, 20 µm across
  • Spin-photon ≥ 65 ± 1 %; spin-photon-photon ≥ 59 ± 2 %, heralded at 0.043 MHz
  • Right: a dot in a waveguide; in the field Bext, Ωr turns its spin and Ωp excites it
  • Its spin-photon Bell state reached 76.3(5) %, post-selected, at 1.3 % efficiency end to end
  • Problem left: the spin keeps its phase only about 33 ns (T2*), even after nuclear spin narrowing
Figures: Coste et al., Nat. Photon. 17, 582 (2023), arXiv:2207.09881, Fig. 1a (left); Meng et al., Nat. Commun. 15, 7774 (2024), arXiv:2310.12038, Fig. 1 (right), CC BY-NC-ND

2.9

Superconducting circuits and transducers

Circuit QED · thermal microwave photons · a cold microwave link · four kinds of transducer · rate and added noise · membranes, step by step · the sideband swap · gigahertz nanobeams · electro-optic crystals · Rydberg atoms · what limits them

2.9

A transmon in a resonator reaches strong coupling easily

  • On the left the resonator, an LC circuit, has evenly spaced levels
  • On the right is the transmon, a Josephson junction beside a capacitor
  • Its cosine well spaces the levels unevenly, so a drive at ωq excites |g⟩ to |e⟩ alone
  • Its dipole, about 104ea0, makes g large
  • The resonator's line splits by 2g/2π=350MHz≫κ/2π≈800kHz
Blais et al., Phys. Rev. A 69, 062320 (2004), arXiv:cond-mat/0402216, Table 1; Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), arXiv:2005.12667, Eqs. 22 and 27; Kurpiers et al., Nature 558, 264 (2018), arXiv:1712.08593; Haroche, Brune and Raimond, Nat. Phys. 16, 243 (2020)
2.9-1

A 5 GHz mode at 300 K holds about 1250 thermal photons

nth=1ehf/kBT−1
  • nth is the mean number of thermal photons in a mode of frequency f
  • At 300 K and 5 GHz, nth≈kBT/hf≈1250
  • The circuits run near 10 mK; their photons cannot leave the refrigerator
  • An optical photon at 194 THz has nth≈3×10−14 even at 300 K
  • A transducer moves the quantum state of a microwave photon onto an optical photon
Haroche, Brune and Raimond, Nat. Phys. 16, 243 (2020)
2.9-2

A cold waveguide joined refrigerators 5 m, then 30 m apart

  • The simplest link needs no conversion: a waveguide kept below 50 mK the whole way
  • In 2020 the refrigerators stood 5 m apart; in 2023, 30 m (pictured)
  • Qubit A emits a photon that B absorbs: a Bell state on every attempt, at 12.5 kHz
  • Fidelity 78.9 % (80.4 % corrected for readout); a loophole-free Bell test gave S=2.0747±0.0033
  • Problem left: it must be cold all the way; to cross a city the photon must become light
Figure: Storz et al., Nature 617, 265 (2023), Fig. 3, CC BY 4.0; Magnard et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 260502 (2020), arXiv:2008.01642; Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), arXiv:2005.12667, pp. 53 and 54
2.9-3

Four kinds of transducer join microwave photons to light

  • (a) Electro-optomechanical transducers couple both modes to a membrane's motion
  • (b) Piezo-optomechanical ones turn the field into a 5.2 GHz phonon in a nanobeam
  • (c) In electro-optic ones the field changes the index of LiNbO3, moving light into the next mode
  • (d) Cold 85Rb atoms in a 100 GHz and a 780 nm cavity convert through their Rydberg states
Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429; Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), arXiv:2004.04838; Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), arXiv:2301.03315; Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), arXiv:2207.10121
2.9-5

A transducer is judged by its photon rate and its added noise

rate=ηt×bandwidth×duty cycle
Nadd=Nout/ηt<1
  • ηt is the efficiency, the fraction of signal photons that leave converted
  • 2 kHz at 50 %, run continuously, equals 20 MHz at 10 % run 6×10−4 of the time
  • The drawing: a beam splitter of transmission ηt, with vacuum entering its unused port
  • Nout is the device's own noise at the output; Nadd refers it to the input, in signal photons
  • Below one added photon a transducer can carry a quantum state
Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429; Zeuthen et al., Quantum Sci. Technol. 5, 034009 (2020), arXiv:1610.01099, Fig. 1b
2.9-6

Membrane transducers cut the added noise from 1500 to 3.2

DeviceWhat was changedEfficiencyAdded noise (photons)
Andrews 2014the first: a membrane between a circuit and an optical cavity, at 4 K8.6 ± 0.7 %about 1500
Higginbotham 2018run in a dilution refrigerator at 35 mK47 ± 1 % at best34 to 38
Brubaker 2022a shielded membrane, cooled by the laser to 0.34 phonons47 ± 1 % at best3.2 ± 0.1, at another setting
  • The simplest kind: one membrane, moved by a circuit's field and read by an optical cavity
  • Its thermal motion leaves as noise; in a 35 mK refrigerator it still held about 1200 phonons
  • The best efficiency and the least noise came at different settings of the two pumps
  • Problem left: 3.2 added photons, still more than one
Andrews et al., Nat. Phys. 10, 321 (2014), arXiv:1310.5276, Fig. 3b; Higginbotham et al., Nat. Phys. 14, 1038 (2018), arXiv:1712.06535, Figs. 2c and 4; Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429
2.9-12

The pumped circuit made the largest part of the 3.2 photons

  • Changed: a shielded membrane and a quieter circuit, run continuously at 40 mK
  • It converted up to 47 ± 1 %, and at another setting added 3.2 ± 0.1 noise photons
  • Of these, 1.4 came from the pumped circuit, 1.0 from the membrane's motion
  • Problem left: the circuit's noise; a 200 nm gap would give 0.9 (predicted)
Figure: Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429, Fig. 1a, CC BY 4.0
2.9-13

A membrane transducer read a transmon without harming it

  • Changed: a transmon (a) was wired (b) to the membrane transducer (c); light detected at (d)
  • The light read the qubit's state in one shot, with a readout fidelity of about 0.4
  • The qubit's coherence time T2 was 20.7±0.2 µs with the laser on, 20.4±0.2 µs off
  • The chain passed 1.9×10−3 of the signal and added 740 photons, mostly circuit noise
  • Problem left: 740 added photons; the 1.45 MHz membrane is slow and warm
Figure: Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022), arXiv:2110.09539, Fig. 1a to 1d
2.9-14

A pump on a sideband swaps or squeezes light and motion

G=g0ncC=4G2κγm
  • A pump of nc photons raises the single-photon coupling g0 to G
  • A pump at ωc−Ωm, the red sideband, swaps light and motion of frequency Ωm
  • At ωc+Ωm, the blue sideband, it makes photon-phonon pairs: two-mode squeezing
  • The swap is quantum when C exceeds nth; κ and the motion's damping γm are full widths
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429
2.9-9

Pumps pass a photon from microwave to motion to light

Ce=4Ge2κeγmCo=4Go2κoγmηt=4CeCo(1+Ce+Co)2
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), arXiv:2112.13429, Eq. 1; Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), arXiv:2004.04838; Meesala et al., Nat. Phys. 20, 871 (2024), arXiv:2303.17684
2.9-10

Gigahertz mechanics added less than one photon of noise

  • Changed: 5.2 GHz mechanics on the qubit's chip, in its ground state at 15 mK
  • The transmon (SC qubit) passed its excitation to one phonon; a laser pulse made it light
  • It converted ηt=(0.88±0.16)×10−5 with Nadd=0.57±0.2, below one
  • Problem left: absorbed light breaks electron pairs; 8 ms to recover, so 100 shots a second
Figure: Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), arXiv:2004.04838, Fig. 1e
2.9-15

Gigahertz devices then gained rate and ran continuously

  • Changed: niobium nitride recovers in nanoseconds: 50 kHz pulses (Meesala 2024)
  • Changed: a silicon nanobeam, coupled by a static voltage, ran continuously (Zhao 2025)
  • The rate is efficiency × bandwidth × duty cycle; the grey band is Nadd<1
  • It converted 2.2 % over 88.9 ± 2.1 kHz at Nadd=0.94: 1.9 kHz of photons
  • Problem left: below one added photon it converted only 2.2 %; more light heats the beam
Zhao et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 20, 602 (2025), arXiv:2406.02704, Fig. 4d and Table II; Meesala et al., Nat. Phys. 20, 871 (2024), arXiv:2303.17684
2.9-7

No moving part: a crystal converted 10 % near one photon

  • Changed: no mechanics; a lithium niobate disk (DUT) in a superconducting cavity at 7 mK
  • A modulator (AOM) cuts the pump, up to about 1 W, into 100 or 300 ns pulses at 5 to 2000 Hz
  • Optics to microwave it added Nadd=1.11−0.07+0.15 photons at 8.0 to 11.4 % efficiency
  • Optical modes 40 times sharper would need 1000 times less pump (projected)
  • Problem left: heat; at 500 Hz the 7 mK stage warmed to at most 60 mK
Figure: Sahu et al., Nat. Commun. 13, 1276 (2022), arXiv:2107.08303, Fig. 1, CC BY 4.0
2.9-16

Electro-optic transducers entangled light and drove a qubit

  • Changed in 2023: a blue-sideband pump makes microwave-optical photon pairs (b)
  • The outputs were 0.72−0.25+0.31 dB (2σ) squeezed: entanglement on every pulse
  • Changed in 2025: on a thin-film chip, light made a tone that drove a transmon
  • It converted ηt=1.18 % over 30 MHz with 44 µW of light
  • Problem left: pump pulses warm the device; the entangling disk ran 2 pulses a second
Figure: Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), arXiv:2301.03315, Fig. 1; Warner et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 831 (2025), arXiv:2310.16155
2.9-17

Rydberg atoms converted 58 % inside, adding 0.6 photons

  • Changed: cold 85Rb atoms, where a 100 GHz niobium cavity crosses a 780 nm cavity, at 5 K
  • Inside, 58(11) % of the photons were converted, over a bandwidth of 360(20) kHz
  • End to end only about 2.5 % arrived: the 100 GHz cavity was coupled out weakly
  • The added noise, 0.6 photons, is the thermal occupation of the 100 GHz mode at 5 K
  • Problem left: it works at 100 GHz, far above a transmon's few gigahertz
Figure: Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), arXiv:2207.10121, Fig. 1a and 1c; Saffman, Walker and Mølmer, Rev. Mod. Phys. 82, 2313 (2010), arXiv:0909.4777, Eq. 6
2.9-18

Heat and noise from the pumps limit today's transducers

  • Absorbed pump light breaks Cooper pairs and heats the device
  • A 154 mW pulse (plot) raised the microwave bath from 0.03 ± 0.01 to 0.09 ± 0.03 photons
  • A strong microwave pump makes the circuit emit noise; cables to a qubit lost 46 %
  • The target for a converter is over 50 % efficiency at a signal-to-noise ratio over 100
  • A heralded pair source keeps its fidelity when photons are lost
Figure: Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), arXiv:2301.03315, Fig. 2D; Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022), arXiv:2110.09539; Warner et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 831 (2025), arXiv:2310.16155; Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson, Science 362, eaam9288 (2018); Meesala et al., Phys. Rev. X 14, 031055 (2024), arXiv:2312.13559

  • The membranes fell from about 1500 added photons (2014) into the box (2018, 2022)
  • The qubit readout (Delaney 2022) is the whole chain, from the qubit's cavity to the detector

2.9-22

Near one added photon, transducers convert 0.5 to 10 %

  • On each grey line the total noise nin, added plus vacuum noise let in by loss, is fixed

2.10-7

Link rates fall by orders of magnitude over distance

R=fPd,P=η2/2
  • The rate is the attempt rate f times the probability per attempt P times the duty cycle d
  • With a two-photon herald P=η2/2, so every loss on the way, fibre included, enters squared
  • The ensembles (Yu 2020) are not plotted: their 1.5 Hz is an estimate
  • The 33 km rate (van Leent 2022) is averaged over the run, reloading included
Data: the papers named at the points; P=η2/2: Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), arXiv:1901.06317
2.10-3

A surface code corrects errors that stay below its threshold

PL~(pb/pbth)d/2+(ps/psth)d/2
  • A patch of d×d data qubits (open circles) holds one logical qubit
  • Check qubits (dots) measure the parity of four neighbours; a bit flip (×) changes two
  • It fails only if errors chain across it, so its logical error PL falls with the distance d (b)
  • pb and ps are the errors of the local gates and of the seam's Bell pairs (pink)
Sinclair et al., Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025), arXiv:2408.08955, Eq. 1; Ramette et al., npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296, Fig. 1b and Eq. 7; curves calculated from the equation
2.7-2

Error correction tolerates noisy pairs but consumes many

  • The seam tolerates about 10 % Bell-pair error at 1 % local error (green, grey; calculated)
  • A distance-20 surface code consumes 40 pairs per cycle and 800 per logical gate
  • 86 pairs at 1 % error, checked as a small code, give one logical pair below 10−10 (calculated)
  • Designs project about 106 pairs per second with one cavity, 5×107 with 30 (orange)
  • Links measured between two atoms (blue) give one pair per 19 s to 208 s
Ramette, npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024), arXiv:2302.01296; Sinclair, Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025), arXiv:2408.08955; Sunami, PRX Quantum 7, 033014 (2026), arXiv:2511.10729; Li and Thompson, PRX Quantum 5, 020363 (2024), arXiv:2401.04075; Hofmann, Science 337, 72 (2012); van Leent, Nature 607, 69 (2022), arXiv:2111.15526

Linked error-corrected modules tolerate per-cent pair errors

  • Local CZ gates reach 99.93 % in superconducting circuits and 99.5 % in tweezer arrays
  • Error correction works up to a pair error of 8.8 % at 1.1 % local error, about 10 % at about 1 %
  • A preprint finds about 13 % at a local error of 0.1 %
  • Only one measured remote pair is below them: 96.89(8) %, heralded, at 9.7 s−1 over 2 m

2.13

Extra slides / Reference material

More results, the comparison tables and the reading, each slide under its own number

2.13

How it works: a measurement on b and c entangles A and D

  • Two pairs: A with b, and c with D; b and c stand in the repeater node
  • A joint measurement on b and c gives one of four results
  • A and D are now entangled, though they never met
  • Two classical bits tell D which result came out
  • The matching correction gives the pair that was wanted
  • It is teleportation: qubit 1 is b, itself half of a pair
Żukowski et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 71, 4287 (1993); Hermans et al., Nature 605, 663 (2022), arXiv:2110.11373
2.5-4

A second click joins two links between clouds

  • L and I₁ share one excitation, and so do I₂ and R: two links
  • Read pulses turn the excitations of I₁ and I₂ into photons that meet on a beam splitter
  • One click leaves L and R sharing one excitation (dashed): a link twice as long
  • A lost photon only makes the click rarer: a link takes T0~tΔ/(ηpp)
  • tΔ is the length of an attempt and ηp the overall efficiency
  • Joined step by step, the time grows as (L/L0)2 for segments of length L0
Duan, Lukin, Cirac and Zoller, Nature 414, 413 (2001), arXiv:quant-ph/0105105, Eq. 6
